text: "Did you hear the news?" shouted Marcus Aurelius as soon as he opened the door and rushed breathlessly into the room.
— What news? — we all called out.
— Bay Ganyo has returned from Europe!
— It can't be!
— How "it cannot be," gentlemen, I saw him, I spoke with him... His first word... ha-ha-ha!... His first word: mess... ha-ha-ha!... We messed it up, he says, we did... ha-ha-ha...
— Stop giggling, — Arpakasha shouted impatiently, — tell us. Do you want tea?
— Arpakash, let me kiss you between your little eyes...
— You ox! — Arpakash let out with a good-natured smile and handed a cup of tea to Marcus Aurelius, pulling him by his curly mustache with his free hand. — Super-ox!
— "Captain, please don't spin the steamship," Marcus Aurelius joked, took a sip from his glass, and told us the following:

— Imagine, gentlemen, what luck, a few days ago, on the 22nd (Alyosha, your favorite number), on Sunday, we went with Gervanich to the Iskar inns, towards Vrazhdebna; we found a whole crowd of people there...
— Weren't the Urvichites there?...

— No, they weren't, they were at their Urvich... Don't interrupt me, Arpakash... There was a crowd of people, mostly foreigners — Germans, Czechs — and not a single one, absolutely not a single one of those Shopi petrified by apathy... Only old man Hadji passed by on his way to his farm. The weather, as you know, was wonderful; those meadows, those fields, that fresh greenery of the forest, you couldn't get enough of breathing it in... The foreigners had come with their whole families, brought along provisions, blankets, cradles for the children; they had sat down here and there like bouquets in the shade and the people were feasting. It was a joy to watch them. And don't think they were some wealthy, affluent people, no, but all craftsmen, working folk — tinsmiths, blacksmiths, carpenters. Work six days — the seventh, revelry! And not like your lordships, huddling in smoky cafes with your cursed "bachka"...
— Marcus Aurelius! Is that you I hear, my little dove? John Chrysostom, let me give you a kiss!...
— Shut up, Arpakash, don't interrupt me...
— Hey, Amonasro, don't interrupt the man — Moishe said.
— But really, gentlemen — Arpakasha continues his joke with a greasy look — tell me, isn't Marcus Aurelius sweet, especially when he pronounces that lovely little word "bachka," it's pure music...
— Will you shut up, Amonasro the Ethiopian?...
— And didn't you notice, gentlemen, what bottomless hatred our sweetest Marcus Aurelius harbors for this woman?
— Listen, Amonasro, shut up or I'll have Moishe pour a whole glass of cognac down your throat.
— But what jok-ers of ours, when they saw grand-ma in pants, ev-ery-one mocked him and did not give him the girl, ta-ra-ra-boom-de-ay, ta-rara boom...
— You are crazy, Arpakash, by God, you are crazy — said Marcus Aurelius with a slight reproach, — stay still for a bit, I beg you...
— Enough already, Arpakash! — the Stinger spoke up.
— And you too, Ozhilka, and you too, Brutus! Go on, sing “Last night I passed by Sevlievo.”
— Down with Arpakasha! — shouted Moishe, and after him the whole company roared "down!" and finally made the Ethiopian king fall silent.
Marcus Aurelius continued:

— No, really, gentlemen, it is a sad phenomenon, this cursed "bachka"; it has petrified us, it has covered our brains with mold and cobwebs. Why, I ask you, I know some friends who for ten whole years — ten years! — gentlemen, this is no joke — have not ceased to rot in the smoky corners of "Panaha" with cards in hand, while before their very noses blooms this beautiful, this picturesque city garden, whose breath and coolness they do not know how to enjoy; and yet outside of Sofia, in the surroundings, what wonderful places! We sit in the cafes and sigh for Switzerland, yet all we need is a little bit of will, and Switzerland, a Bulgarian Switzerland, is before us — Vitosha, Rila, the Rhodopes! The lowliest poor foreigner living in Sofia has enjoyed the majestic view from Cherni Vrah on Vitosha, but tell me, is there even one — one, good heavens! — Shop who has climbed Vitosha! We know examples among Italian workers who have left ready work here just because they grew tired of the monotony and, at risk, set off to wander to see the world; and yet, on the other hand, there are examples like, let's say, the shepherd of the Dragalevtsi Monastery, who all his life has looked down upon the city of Sofia from the heights, looked at it years before the Liberation, looked at its destruction, its renewal and expansion, and continues to gaze even now, sitting under the shade of the walnut tree, at its more glamorous appearance, and to this day he has no will to come down from the forest to be curious, to see up close this transformation of the capital, interesting in every respect!... But I justify this peculiar philosopher and even, to tell you the truth, I envy this child of nature! But what can I say about many of our wealthy citizens, who choke all their lives in the dust, smells, and miasmas of Sofia's old streets, look all their lives at the beautiful Dragalevtsi woods and have not had the will to get up, to go there and enjoy its breath and coolness, the enchanting sound of the foaming stream, and the nightingales...
— Well now, you’ve turned out to be quite the poet, Marcus Aurelius, look at that!... But tell me, why are you telling us these old wives’ tales; aren’t you supposed to be telling us about Bay Ganyo?

— That is why I am telling you "old wives' tales," because it simply infuriates me to see what kind of apathy has stiffened us... To say that we do not appreciate natural beauties—no; we cannot fail to appreciate them, because it is a natural feeling—even the cattle appreciate it; but the thing is, we are frozen by Eastern immobility. If I grab you by the collar, Arpakash, and drag you toward the Urvich Monastery, once I lead you behind the Kokalyane hill over the Iskar abyss and you hear the mysterious speech of the winding, foaming river, you will start clicking your tongue and you will cry out, you will surely cry out: "My, it is a whole Switzerland! Look, our Bulgaria was beautiful, and we, fools, did not know it, but spend our holidays soaking in the cafes." But as soon as you return to Sofia and breathe its stifling atmosphere, you will fall back into lethargy, apathy will petrify you again, until someone else drags you by the collar.

Now — about Bay Ganyo. Gervanich and I spent the whole day roaming through the woods, rolling on the grass among the trees, eating, drinking, staring at the merry groups of foreigners who had surrendered themselves body and soul to the festivities; they had organized various games, were singing, running, jumping — you'd envy them! Towards evening, after a delicious snack, Gervanich and I went into the inn to have coffee. At one point, bells were heard from the direction of the Orhanie road, and after a while, a phaeton with passengers appeared in a cloud of dust. One passenger got out of the carriage, then a second, and from behind the driver's back, the voice of the third was heard: “Bay Mihal, take the saddlebags; mind you don't bump them somewhere, don't break the vials, for we'll have nothing to show for ourselves before... that person.”

And after those words, out of the carriage jumped... Bay Ganyo. The same Bay Ganyo, just as you know him, before he set off for Europe; with the only difference being that he had put on a tie and, besides that, now possessed an imposing appearance and a sense of self-dignity and superiority over those around him. The man had seen it all across Europe; Europe had become to him like... like nothing. He gave his left mustache a tug, cleared his throat into his palm, and scanned in a semicircle, with the kind of look our policemen give to prisoners, the groups of merrymaking foreigners; and having cast an eye and shaken his head at his ignorant companions, as if he wanted to say to them: "I could weep for you," he sighed deeply and uttered significantly: "Eh, Prater, Prater!"
— What did you say, your honor, I couldn't quite hear — spoke up the man called Bai Michal.

— I could weep for you while you're still living — Bay Ganyo uttered compassionately. — Oh, Prater, Prater!... Has it ever crossed your minds what a thing that Prater is! But how could it ever cross your minds. And if I were to start telling you — you wouldn't be able to understand it.

And to show those of his simple companions who were capable of understanding him, he approached one of the merrymaking groups, near which several drained beer barrels were rolling, and with an ironic smile, gestured with his eyes toward the grove and uttered: "Das ist bulgarische Prater, ha-ha-ha!..."

The entire group, their eyes merrily clouded by beer, looked our "German" up and down, and one of the company, without heeding Bay Ganyo’s ironic remark, handed him a glass of flat wine with the words: — We invite you, sir, do you want beer?
"Even these don't understand me," thought Bay Ganyo, and as he returned to his companions, he added: "They've gotten drunk as... Cossacks."

After that, the group entered the tavern and sat down near us. I had my back to them and Bay Ganyo could not recognize me; and that he did not recognize me was evident from the words he let slip at our expense: "These ones must have gotten plastered too. German stock!"
The servant approached the travelers and began to wipe the table:
— Don't you want something? — he asked.
— We don't want any, we have our own. But, oh well, never mind, give me some water and a light: pour some fresh water — ordered Bai Ganyo.
Among the passengers, a mysterious, serious conversation began, from which not all words reached us.
— Tonight we'll hardly see the big man, it will be late — whispered Bay Ganyo, — we'll send him the gifts and send him word for tomorrow; then he will arrange for us when to go to the prince.
— And what about a gift for the prince? — Uncle Mihal asked cautiously.

— No need — Bay Ganyo answers authoritatively, — here everything is the big man; if you pull the wool over his eyes — you'll end up in your underwear. We will give him what the lawyer wrote for us to read and if there is something to correct — that's his business! Mind your behavior before the Prince, hey, don't let anyone get scared. You watch me and what I do. When I say, as they told us to say: “Your Royal Highness, God forbid you accept his resignation, lest it becomes the Trans-Danubian Province,” then you follow after me: “God forbid, Your Royal Highness!”
— Of course, what else can we say — Bai Mihal replies submissively.
— Hey you, Mihal, you smell a bit like a boot, who knows what you're up to? Keep your wits about you! — warns Bai Ganyo patronizingly.
— Who? Me? — Bai Mihal justifies himself. — Don't say that, brother, someone will hear. Even the walls have ears. When I hear the name "Cossack," I get the shivers.

— You're getting the shakes, aren't you? — Bay Ganyo whispered softly, with a wink. — And when the Russians came, who plundered the cattle from the Turkish villages, eh? Since when have you had these riches, eh? Come on, tell me!
— But you too, Bay Ganyo, let's speak the truth — whispers Bay Michal — didn't the mills remain yours from the Russian time? Tell me, isn't that so?
— Come on, come on, one can't even have a word with you. What was, was. Now it's not like that. Now it's the Trans-Danubian Governorate, do you understand?
— Why, of course I understand! — said Uncle Michal and gave a devilish wink to his companions.
And all three laughed into their hands so that no one would hear them.
— Whoa, get your wits about you, watch out, for if someone hears you—we’re headed for trouble... Hey, boy, what’s that newspaper there? "Svoboda"? — Bay Ganyo turned to the servant.
— “Free speech,” sir.
— Oh, how I’d like to read a bit — whispers Bay Ganyo to his companions, — but I’m afraid, damn it. The big shot will hear — and then go try to explain yourself.

But just at that moment, a scene occurred that made the passengers freeze in their places. A five- or six-year-old boy was stepping lazily around the threshold of the tavern, singing some improvisations to himself and, apparently under the impression of the three-day continuous "down with" in Sofia to the tune of "Shumi Maritsa," he abandoned the actual lyrics and, absorbed in his song, used the following words ingrained in his brain: "Down-wn-wn, down, down-wn-wn, down, do-o-own, do-o-own, down Stambolov!" A chorus of laughter from the merrymaking groups interrupted the child's improvisation, who, excited by the unexpected success, again, with a louder voice, almost a scream, continued his song and instead of "ma-arch, ma-arch!" — shouted "do-own, do-own, down Stambolov, do-do-do-do-own, down Stambolov." This time, besides the collective laughter, applause and shouts of "bravo," "down," "down with the libertine," "down with the tyrant" were heard from a group of young people returning from a walk.
I turned toward the table of the three passengers.

Bai Ganyo and his companions turned into statues. With mouths agape, with eyes staring motionlessly, their faces depicted such a mournful mixture of fear and astonishment that I could do nothing but regret not having a camera... Bai Ganyo was the first to come to his senses, turned his eyes toward the demonstrators, and immediately shuddered, as if struck by an electric current: a mounted police guard was passing along the road and hearing these terrible shouts, and instead of drawing his saber and, like a whirlwind with a furious cry, brandishing it around the heads of these unheard-of rebels, these black souls, these brigands and traitors, he looked on calmly, with a good-natured smile on his face... If a volcano had erupted on Vitosha at that moment, it could hardly have stunned our travelers more than this scene...

"— We've botched it, we have! — Bay Ganyo uttered with a desperate sigh. — Hey, Bay Mihal, go over by the counter, please, and take a peek at 'Svobodno Slovo,' see if you can figure out what this business is all about..."
— That’s a fine thing, but why don’t you go? Let’s see your courage! — replied Uncle Michal.

— Hey, you're so simple! What would it hurt to finally take a peek; pass by the counter, as if you're looking at the rakia, whistling to yourself like that, and with one eye, just like that, see... if there isn't a new minis... God forbid!...
— Impossible... Use your head!...
— Didn't you see the policeman?... Wait a minute, I'm not afraid—I'll take a look at the newspaper, and to hell with it!

And Bay Ganyo rose from his seat, began whistling "Green Leaf" through his teeth, and while looking around as if absent-mindedly, made an eagle's circle toward the counter; he approached, grabbed a bottle of cognac by the neck and, pretending to read its label, squinted his eyes so far to the right that a person facing him would see only their whites, and his gaze fell upon the folded newspaper, of which only the title "Svobodno Slovo" was visible. He shuffled his right hand and, intensifying "Green Leaf" to drown out the rustling of the paper, opened one part of it and, with eyes horribly twisted to the right, read: "News from the Palace. Today... presented himself to H. R. Highness the Prime Minister and Minister of Internal Affairs, Mr. Dr. K. Stoil..." — Something caught in Bay Ganyo's throat; he coughed; instantly licked his dry lips and cast a squinted eye further down and read in large capital letters: "Stambol has fallen...", and Ganyo's heart sank into his boots, he dropped the bottle of cognac and, to cover the noise produced, began to cough loudly... Bay Ganyo turned to his companions and uttered significantly: — He's finished!
— Good luck, Bay Ganyo! — called out Bay Mihal.
— It’s all over! — added Bay Ganyo and, as he approached the table, whispered quietly to his companions: — Stambolov Effendi is finished! Stoilov now...
— It can't be, man, what are you saying! In the newspaper?...
— Of course!
— Hey, could it be some kind of fabrication?
— What a fabrication! — Bai Ganyo cried out, and gathering all his courage, he pounded on the table and shouted: — Hey, boy, bring "Svobodno Slovo" over here...
The comrades involuntarily lowered their heads and began to look around timidly.

The boy brought the newspaper and happened to hand it to Bai Mihal, but he, as if being handed red-hot iron, pulled back his hand and gestured with his eyes toward Bai Ganyo. Bai Ganyo took the paper and, as is well known, turned around to see what was and wasn't happening in the tavern, for after all, where would Bai Ganyo find so much courage! But a brave man nonetheless! He unfolded "Svobodno Slovo" and began: "Stamb[olov] has fallen..."

Bay Ganyo began to cough, his companions began to cough even more loudly. Bay Michal squinted his eye toward the newspaper to see if his brave companion was reading correctly and was convinced that there was no mistake... The third companion also bowed his head toward the newspaper and read and... a fever shook him, and his head began to spin. How many of his deeds and misdeeds, slumbering for years under the prosecutor's cloth, would those two little words drag out into the light of day...
With huddling, with whispering, with coughing, they devoured the editorial, and having glanced here and there through the newspaper, they learned and were finally convinced that the job was done.
— We've made a mess of it! Now what? It's too late now to beg that his resignation not be accepted. To hell with it. Well, Mihal, why are you silent? Tell me, what's to be done? — asks Bay Ganyo.
— Speak, your honor; I am so stunned, as if someone had struck me over the noggin with a club — Bai Michal replies desperately.
— And what about you, Gunyo, why are you silent? You say something too. What are we to do now, eh?
— Well, how should I know... Whatever you say, your grace — mumbles the dejected Gunyo.

— Why, don't you have any sense, you fool! Is it always up to me to set you right — cries Bay Ganyo, almost moved to tears with despair, — anyway, come on, let me teach you this time as well... Do you know what?

On this matter Bay Ganyo pondered with a frown, scratched himself where it didn't itch, coughed once or twice into his palm, reached into the pocket of his frock coat, took out a piece of paper folded in four, and handed it to Bay Gunyo.
— Go ahead and read that damn thing once more, and then I'll tell you what we're going to do.
— But why, your grace, don't you read it?
— But, Gunyo, don't provoke me! You know why I don't read it; it comes more naturally to you to read those papist words...

Gunyo unfolded the paper and read more or less the following: “Your Royal Highness! Heavenly thunders have showered upon our unfortunate heads! Our five-century slavery is a pleasant dream compared to the hideous blow that the Northern enemy deals us through the resignation of our—oh! are there words!—most brilliant leader, this Cicero, this Newton of the Bulgarian firmament! O tempora, o mores!

“No, Your Royal Highness! We still believe in the common sense of the valiant Bulgarian people and expect that they will not part with the man who is the personification of their aspirations and ideals, of everything honest, noble, chaste, progressive, liberal! We will not believe that Your Royal Highness will entrust the power into the hands of those debauched traitors, those ignorant and ill-bred nonentities, who day and night strive to undermine the foundations of our state system and to throw our dear fatherland under the stinking boot of the Cossack.

Your Royal Highness! Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes! The above resolution was adopted by 11,000 of the most prominent citizens, and Ganyo Balkanski, Michal Michalev, and Gunyo Kilipirchikov were authorized to present it at the feet of Your Royal Highness. Hurrah!

"Hey, what a shoddy people we are!" says Bay Ganyo, shaking his head and clicking his tongue. "When it comes to lying, the old Gypsies are nothing compared to us. Can it really go that far? 11,000 most prominent citizens! Ha-ha-ha! Take away the thousands, how many are left?"
— Eleven people — Michal answers.
— Were there only that many?
— Well, that’s it, Bay Ganyo, right is right. Didn’t I go with a policeman to collect them?

— Wretched people!... Now, do you know what? There can be no talk of going back. You, Gunyo, are a bit of a lawyer. Roll up your sleeves, please, and let's all together concoct another address for the new one... No, I have paper. And let's hope they don't find out we came to plead for that fine fellow, or we're finished. Especially your business, Gunyo... If another prosecutor comes.
Gunyo cleared his throat... "Give me the paper and the pencil," he said anxiously. "You watch, I will write."
And he began to write: "Your Royal Highness! Heavenly thunders showered upon our unhappy heads!..."
— Now we must write it backwards. How shall we write it?... Wait... Do you approve of it like this: “The heavens opened and showered grace upon our fatherland.”
— "Just 'fatherland' sounds too plain," declares Bay Ganyo, "put 'our dear fatherland'."
— I also think that without love it is worth nothing — says Uncle Michal.

— Good, I’ve put it, my dear. Further on: “Our five-century slavery is a pleasant dream compared to the hideous blow”... Now the other way around: “Our liberation from our five-century slavery is nothing compared to the brilliant event that shattered the chains of the hideous tyrant.” Do you agree?
— You should have added "spawn of hell" as well — states Bay Ganyo. — But never mind, later.
— ...'which the Northern enemy inflicts upon us through the resignation of our — oh! are there words! — most brilliant leader, this Cicero, this Newton of the Bulgarian horizon.'

— Now, how shall we turn this?... Wait... Here is how: “And which is due solely to Your Royal Highness, most merciful father and sire, by accepting the resignation of this — oh! are there words — most hideous tormentor, this Caligula, this Tamerlane of the Bulgarian horizon.”
— Bravo, Gunyo! — Bay Ganyo cried out with eyes shining with enthusiasm.
— Well, what do you think, Gunya? — Mihal coaxed.

— “O tempora, o mores!”... That can stay. Wherever you put it, it’s always in its place... “No, Your Royal Highness!”... Let’s put: “Yes, Your Royal Highness!... We still believe in the common sense of the valiant Bulgarian people and expect that they will not part with the man...” Now, instead of “will not part with,” we’ll put “and will wipe off the face of the earth,” and instead of “the man,” we’ll put “the ferocious beast.”
— No, better put "the mad monster" — Bay Ganyo corrects.
— I, for one, think we should put "Fiery Gehenna" — said Michal.
— Oh, you really stuck it to him! Ha-ha-ha! Why on earth "fiery Gehenna"? Better to put "the dirty bloodsucker" — says Gunyo.
— Ha, do you see now! Bravo! — Bay Ganyo approved.

— ...'who is the personification of its aspirations and ideals — of everything honest, noble, chaste, progressive, liberal!' Now let's turn it inside out... 'who is the personification of the people's misfortune!... of everything dishonest, vagabondish, depraved, obscurantist, and tyrannical!' Further on: 'We shall not believe that Your Royal Highness will entrust the power into the hands of those depraved traitors, those ignorant and ill-bred nonentities...' How shall we flip it now?... Wait! It came to me! Here is how: 'Allow us, Your Royal Highness, to consider ourselves fortunate and to express our most boundlessly loyal feelings, for having entrusted the power into the hands of those noble patriots, those educated and well-bred statesmen... who strive day and night to undermine the foundations of our state system.'
— How so! You're mistaken! — said Bay Ganyo, startled.
— Now we will turn it inside out, so instead of "to undermine" we will put "to strengthen." "And to throw our dear fatherland under the stinking boot of the Cossack."

— Let's see now — says Bay Ganyo. — Now is the crunch! We don't know, damn it, how the current ones will handle things with Muscovy. If a man knew they wanted to make peace — easy job, we could write a heap of things: “Tsar Liberator; Tsar Protector; brothers from the same womb; the scabby German kikes” and so on; but we don't know which way the wind will blow... Fine: “Slavic brothers,” but what if the current ones are against the Slavs, and then look... hop! — Bay Ganyo is a traitor! No, you know what? Better to throw out that bit about the “smelly boot”...
— Well, what shall we put!...

— Wai-it! Don't hurry! We'll think... You know what? Now, since we don't know yet which way the wind is blowing, let's put it both this way and that way, and let them interpret it however it suits them. Let's put it like this... "And let us embrace as brothers both with the Russians and with the Germans... Phooey! May God strike them!..."
— No, it doesn't suit at all like that! What is this "both-and"? Is that how one speaks before a prince! — declares the lawyering Gunyo.

— And how should one talk then, you brat! Are you going to teach me! — Bay Ganyo flared up. — Do you know who I am? Do you know that I have traversed all of Europe? I am not a blockhead like you! Do you know that this Jireček-Mireček, just like that—they listened to me with their mouths agape when I started talking to them. Englishmen, Americans have shown me respect in Dresden... so are you going to teach me sense?... Do you know that I...
— I know, Bai Ganyo, how could I not know — the startled Gunyo justifies himself.
— Well, since you know, what’s all that... Anyway, write it there as you know how...
— Let us write it like this: "...and to place us, if not higher, then at least alongside the great European powers"...
— Well, I agree — Bay Ganyo approves.
— ...“with the great European powers, by returning us to the greatness of Asparuh and Krum.”
— I agree. Fine.
— Now, moving on: “Your Royal Highness, Timeo danaos et dona ferentes!” ...Instead of it, it’s best to put: “Vox populi, vox dei.” Do you agree?
— Finally, well, so be it, put it in. It’s not exactly Bulgarian, but if it must be, what can we do about it! — Bay Ganyo agrees.
— ...'The above resolution was adopted by 11 thousand of the most prominent citizens, and Ganyo Balkanski was authorized...' and so forth, this can remain intact until the end.
— Should we leave them at only 11 thousand people, or should we increase it by another one or two thousand for the sake of the new ones? Should we grease their wheels?
— That's enough, Bai Ganyo. In our town, even if you gather the blind and the lame, it's unlikely they'll reach 11,000, but oh well, never mind, it's for the sake of a favor, after all!
— I agree... But look... instead of Ganyo Balkanski, wouldn't it be more dignified to put "Mr. Ganyo" and so forth? So the Prince can see that we aren't some low-class people, eh?
— I'll say the same — Michal speaks up.
— Efendiler, it's late. Let's go! — shouted the Turkish coachman from the threshold of the tavern. The passengers left for Sofia.

The next day, gentlemen, I read in one of the local newspapers that a deputation from the town of P., consisting of Ganyo Balkanski and so forth, had presented itself before the great gates to give thanks for the liberation from the tyrannical regime.

Two days later, in this newspaper, I read a telegram from the same city, signed in the name of “thousands” of citizens, with which they informed the dignitaries that Bai Ganyo and his comrades were a self-appointed deputation and that the actual representatives of the people had already set off for the capital to express their gratitude...

I knew the hotel where Bay Ganyo was staying, and I headed towards it. I did not want to express indignation at his vile act, not because any indignation would be too pale to condemn it; but I wished to make an attempt — to see if it were possible to make this unfortunate child of circumstances realize the full horror of his deed.

On the hotel board, I read which room Bay Ganyo was in and climbed the stairs. I knocked on the door; no one answered. I pressed the handle and the door opened. The room was empty. They had left. On the table, I caught sight of a scrap of paper on which was written in Bay Ganyo’s handwriting: "To the editorial office of the newspaper 'Free Word'." The latter name was crossed out, and in its place was written "Freedom." Further down: "The Secrets of Stambolov" — this too was crossed out, and instead was written "Anarchy." It was clearly visible that the author of the letter had hesitated for a long time over which path to take, for on many lines one could notice crossed-out words replaced by others completely opposite to them in meaning. For example, "patriots" was written and crossed out, and above it was written "daylight robbers" — this too was crossed out, and "patriots" was written once again. The entire letter was crossed out crosswise with thick lines drawn by an angry hand; because the ink had failed for the second stroke, the pen had been dipped once more and a line twice as thick had been drawn... Beneath the crossed-out lines stood the following words: "You’ve turned us into monkeys, may the devil take you, you scoundrels..."
